title: When the Blue Hour Sings
premise: Wren Okonkwo, a night librarian in a sleepless city, has spent ten years guarding a secret: the songs his late mother wrote but never recorded, and the one untranslatable sentence she left in her notebook. When he hears one of those songs playing on the radio—recorded by a stranger who claims to have written it—his careful invisibility shatters. As Wren investigates the theft, he uncovers the truth about his mother's life before him and the father he never knew, forcing him to choose between protecting her memory and telling the truth that could destroy the man who stole it. In the end, Wren translates the sentence aloud at a memorial concert, claiming both his inheritance and his own voice.
about_author: Wren Sandoval is the pen name of a former night-shift archivist who spent years cataloguing other people's letters before writing any of their own. They live in a coastal city where the fog arrives earlier every year, and they still can't sleep before three in the morning.

chapters.title: The Hours That Belong to No One
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. We meet him shelving books at 3 a.m., navigating a city that never quite sleeps, and practicing the small evasions that define him: almost-sentences, unfinished emails, a phone call to his aunt he keeps not making. Emotional beat: comfortable loneliness beginning to itch.

chapters.title: Songs Without Owners
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. At home, he opens his mother Amara's battered songbook for the thousandth time without reading past the first page. Flashback fragments of her humming establish the depth of his avoidance. Beat: tenderness laced with dread.

chapters.title: A Voice on the Frequency
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Driving home at dawn, the radio plays a song he knows note for note—one Amara wrote and never recorded. The DJ credits a singer named Cass Meridian. Wren pulls over, shaking. Beat: the world cracks open.

chapters.title: What the Notebook Wouldn't Say
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He finally reads the songbook cover to cover and finds, on the last page, a single sentence in Amara's handwriting—in Igbo, untranslated, addressed to someone unnamed. Beat: grief reorganized as mission.

chapters.title: The Man Who Sings Like Her
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. He tracks Cass Meridian to a small venue and watches from the back. Cass performs two more of Amara's songs. Wren nearly confronts him and fails. Beat: cowardice that costs something.

chapters.title: Auntie Ngozi's Long Memory
chapters.summary: Ngozi's POV. Wren visits his aunt, who recognizes the songbook instantly and goes quiet. She reveals Amara had a collaborator once—a man named Theo—and warns Wren that some truths are heavier than silence. Beat: the past acquires a shape.

chapters.title: Backstage, Almost
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren gets backstage under a borrowed press badge, stands face to face with Cass, and says nothing—instead asking for an autograph like a fan. That night he can't sleep at all. Beat: self-disgust sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: Ten Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A flashback chapter: how Amara died, how Wren abandoned music school afterward, how invisibility became a discipline. We understand why the sentence terrifies him. Beat: compassion for his own fear.

chapters.title: Theo's Address
chapters.summary: Ngozi's POV. Ngozi gives Wren a name and an old address, confessing she helped Amara disappear from Theo's life—and from hers. Beat: loyalty revealed as complicity.

chapters.title: The Thief's Apartment
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren finds Theo living modestly, surrounded by demo tapes. Theo recognizes him instantly—'You have her hands'—and admits he recorded the songs after Amara's death, believing they were left to him. Beat: certainty collapses.

chapters.title: Two Claimants
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Theo tells his version: he and Amara wrote together; the songs were theirs. Wren hears Amara's voice in Theo's stories and hates how much he believes it. Beat: the binary of thief/hero dissolves.

chapters.title: Cass Learns the Truth
chapters.summary: Cass's POV. Wren sends Cass a copy of the songbook page dated years before Theo's recordings. Cass, shaken, meets Wren secretly; she'd been told the songs were Theo's originals. Beat: an unlikely alliance forms.

chapters.title: The Untranslatable Sentence
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren takes the sentence to an elderly Igbo scholar, who explains it resists translation because it holds a double meaning: a farewell and an accusation at once. Wren must decide which meaning is true. Beat: language itself becomes the antagonist.

chapters.title: What Ngozi Withheld
chapters.summary: Ngozi's POV. Pressed by Wren, Ngozi admits the sentence was written to her—the accusation half—and that she chose silence to protect Amara's legend. Wren leaves furious. Beat: betrayal inside the family.

chapters.title: Radio Silence
chapters.summary: Cass's POV. Theo threatens to bury Cass's career if she speaks; her label wavers. Cass must choose between the career she built on stolen ground and the truth. Beat: rising external pressure.

chapters.title: The Archive at Night
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Working nights in the library's special collections, Wren finds Amara's old copyright registration—filed jointly with Theo, then amended to her name alone. The legal truth is messier than either story. Beat: hope complicated by evidence.

chapters.title: Confrontation in the Blue Hour
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Wren and Cass confront Theo together with the documents. Theo breaks down: he didn't steal so much as refuse to let Amara vanish, and the recordings were his mourning. Beat: climax of truth-telling; no villain survives intact.

chapters.title: The Sentence, Spoken
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren finally translates the sentence aloud—to Ngozi, then to himself: 'You kept me singing when I wanted to stop, and I forgive you for what it cost.' Grief and love arrive in the same breath. Beat: emotional climax.

chapters.title: Credit Where Due
chapters.summary: Cass's POV. Cass announces publicly that the songs were co-written by Amara Okonkwo and Theo Marsh, pledging royalties to a music fund in Amara's name. Theo accepts neither credit nor forgiveness gracefully. Beat: justice as repair, not victory.

chapters.title: The Memorial Concert
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At a small hall, Cass performs the songs with Theo accompanying; Wren reads Amara's lyrics and, for the first time, sings one himself, badly and bravely. Ngozi sits in the front row. Beat: inheritance claimed publicly.

chapters.title: Daylight Hours
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Weeks later, Wren requests a transfer to day shifts, finishes the letter to a music school he abandoned ten years ago, and lets the songbook rest closed on his shelf—not hidden, just finished. Beat: quiet transformation.

chapters.title: When the Blue Hour Sings
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. On the anniversary of Amara's death, Wren walks the city at dawn as the radio plays her credited song. He hums along, out loud, unembarrassed, and writes the first line of a song of his own. Beat: resolution—the invisible man, visible at last.
